transcript: are you Team Sondheim or Team Audra? …is maybe the worst question you could ask a musical theatre fan but when Stephen Sondheim took shots at Audra McDonald in the press along with two of her acclaimed collaborators it might have been a rare case when the great Stephen Sondheim was actually wrong… Though maybe not entirely. welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history in August of 2011 rehearsals were underway for a new Broadway version of Porgy and Bess that essentially aimed to adapt this classic American opera into a piece of musical theatre the adaptation was being written by Pulitzer Prize winner Suzan-Lori Parks under the direction of Diane Paulus and of course boasting an incredibly stacked cast led by Audra McDonald and Norm Lewis and Patrick Healy for the New York Times sat in on these rehearsals for the out of town tryout to discuss some of the changes being made to the material. the contents of this article sent Stephen Sondheim into a bit of a rage so he submitted a pretty scathing and snarky response letter to the New York Times condemning the comments of Paulus, Parks, and even his friend Audra McDonald Paulus had said “in the opera you don't really get to know many of the characters as people” “especially and most problematically Bess” and went on to say “I'm sorry but to ask an audience these days to invest three hours in a show” “requires having your heroine be an understandable and fully rounded character” to which Sondheim replied “that's willful ignorance,” “these characters are as vivid as any ever created for the musical theatre” “if she doesn't understand Bess and feels she has to excavate the show” “she clearly thinks it's a ruin, so why is she doing it?” “I'm sorry, but could the problem be her lack of understanding?” Suzan-Lori Parks had said about her adaptation “I wanted to flesh out the two main characters so they're not cardboard cut outs” “I think that's what George Gershwin wanted” “and if he had lived longer, he would have gone back to the story of Porgy and Bess” “and made some changes” Sondheim replied “it's reassuring that Ms. Parks has a direct pipeline to Gershwin” “and is just carrying out his work for him” and Audra McDonald had said of the character of Bess “she's often more of a plot device than a full blooded character” Sondheim: “often? meaning sometimes she's full blooded and other times not?” “she's always full blooded when she's acted full bloodedly” McDonald: “the opera has the makings of a great love story too” “that I think we're bringing to life wow” Sondheim: “who would have thought there was a love story hiding in Porgy and Bess” “that just needed a group of visionaries to bring it out?” there's a lot more to the letter, but you get the idea. though notably, one of the things he took issue with most was the proposal to give the musical a more happy ending and after Sondheim’s diatribe, they did end up restoring the original ending though Diane Paulus insisted with an understandable hint of resentment “it had nothing to do with Mr. Whomever-we're-not-talking-about” “I'm reluctant to talk about the details of the ending” “because frankly, I don't want it to get misinterpreted” “I don't want someone to read it and go crazy” cause they were making a lot of changes  before, during, and after the tryout to tinker with it and find that balance one such change that I was just looking for an excuse to mention is that the Cambridge production used real life babies played by the twin children of Tony nominated cast member Natasha Yvette Williams but they were replaced with a doll on Broadway because they got “a little rambunctious.” but I digress! when asked about the Sondheim incident by Terry Gross, Audra McDonald said: “it didn't feel great to get, you know, kind of slapped around by Sondheim in such a public fashion” “but at the same time I know my relationship with Steve” “and my relationship with Steve is” “you know, despite this letter, still, I think, a positive one.” at first glance it seems that history proved Sondheim at least partly wrong: the Broadway reviews were mixed to positive but it did win the Tony for Best Revival it went on tour and they achieved their goal of introducing at least one wide-eyed 16- year-old theatre fan to this seminal work, in a way that felt digestible. but Sondheim admitted he wasn't saying the production would be bad or unsuccessful he was not “judging this production in advance” “only the attitude of its creators toward the piece and the audience.” “perhaps it will be wonderful” “perhaps Ms. Paulus and company will have earned their arrogance.” and I do agree with some of what he was saying not least of which is that it is more than a little ironic that they literally changed the name of the show to “the Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess,” but also, when approaching any adaptation process I do think that it should come from a place of love for the source material and at the very least it might not be the best PR strategy to imply otherwise. having said that, it's very possible that this profile cherry picked some of the more pointed quotes that were part of a larger conversation about the creative process with more shades of nuance and admiration McDonald even said as much herself in the Terry Gross interview. she said: “even if that's how it came across within the piece” “there is not one Iota of disdain for this opera in my heart.” the other elephant in the room here is that we're essentially talking about two Black women, and one white woman talking specifically about how they wanted to flesh out this Black female protagonist. then you have Sondheim not only dismissing their concerns and saying “you just don't understand Bess” but being unnecessarily nasty about it by any standard. and while he might not have been trying to pre-judge the material it certainly had that effect; McDonald said: “it could have been very damaging to us” “we had people coming to review the show on the first preview” “a couple people came to the show with Sondheim’s letter in their hand” “asking questions afterward, shaking the letter at us” but fittingly the conclusion to this unpleasant saga was summed up perfectly by McDonald herself: “at the end of the day we made it to Broadway” “and, you know I'm still singing Sondheim, and we move on”
classificationReason: Historical retrospective about the 2011 Broadway Porgy and Bess and the Sondheim vs. Audra McDonald/Diane Paulus controversy. No first-hand review of the production; the 2011 Porgy and Bess is also not in the provided show list.
